angle: you're the analyst; spies say 1,400 tanks a month; read the serial numbers of 4 captured tanks (19, 40, 42, 60); the biggest is a floor, not the answer (alone it lands a fifth too low); 56 unseen numbers / 4 gaps = 14, add one more gap: 74; real WWII: 246 vs spies' 1,400 vs records 245; reveal: the German tank problem
title: How to count enemy tanks from 4 serial numbers
description:
Every captured tank carries a serial number. Capture 4 with numbers 40, 42, 60 and 19: there are 56 numbers below 60 you never saw, spread over 4 gaps, so about 14 per gap. Add one more gap above the biggest and you get 74 tanks. Use the biggest number alone and you'd be about a fifth too low on average. Allied statisticians did this in World War II with gearbox serial numbers: they estimated 246 tanks a month, intelligence said 1,400, and German records later showed 245. It's known as the German tank problem.

Numbers checked in code (the formula m + m/k - 1, plus 200,000 simulated captures). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_tank_problem
facts_checked: 4 captured serials 40, 42, 60, 19: 56 unseen numbers below 60, 14 per gap, estimate 60 + 14 = 74 = m + m/k - 1 (verify.py)
With 4 captures, the biggest serial alone averages 80% of the true total (a fifth too low); the formula is right on average (verify.py, 200,000 simulated captures)

WWII, June 1940 - Sept 1942: statistical estimate 246 a month, intelligence 1,400, German records 245; gearbox serial numbers were the main ones used: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_tank_problem

beats.say: You're a war analyst, and your spies swear the enemy builds 1,400 tanks a month. You need the real number. Here's how you get it.
Ignore the spies. Go look at the tanks you've captured. Every gearbox has a serial number, stamped in order.
Say you've captured 4. Their numbers are 40, 42, 60, and 19.
So the enemy has built at least 60. But uh-oh. The biggest one you caught is almost never the last one built. Stop there, and you'll be about a fifth too low.
So look at the gaps. Below 60, there are 56 numbers you never saw, spread over 4 gaps. That's 14 per gap.
Now assume one more gap of 14 sits above your biggest. 60 plus 14. Your answer is 74.
Do this with every tank you capture. Your math says 246 tanks a month. The spies still say 1,400.
And there you have it. After the war, the enemy's own records come out. They built 245.
This is the German tank problem. Allied statisticians did exactly this in World War Two, and beat their own spies.
